questions.q: Which statement best defines nuclear fusion?
options: The splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller, more stable fragments
The process of joining two smaller nuclei together to form a larger, more stable nucleus
The emission of an alpha particle from an unstable nucleus
The capture of a slow-moving neutron by a uranium nucleus
questions.explanation: Nuclear fusion is the process of joining two smaller nuclei together to form a larger, more stable nucleus, releasing energy. It was first observed by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant in 1932, who fired a fast heavy hydrogen nucleus at a heavy hydrogen target to produce a nucleus of tritium plus an extra neutron.

questions.q: On the graph of average binding energy per nucleon against mass number, which nucleus is the most stable, and what does this imply about joining together light nuclei?
options: Hydrogen-1 is most stable; fusing light nuclei always absorbs energy
Iron-56 is the most stable nucleus; joining light nuclei produces nuclei with a higher average binding energy per nucleon, so energy is released
Uranium-238 is most stable; fusion only releases energy for heavy nuclei
Helium-4 is most stable; both fusion and fission consume energy
questions.explanation: The graph of average binding energy per nucleon against mass number shows the most stable nuclei have a mass number of about 50 to 60, and the most stable nucleus is in fact iron-56. If we join together light nuclei we produce nuclei with a higher average binding energy per nucleon, so energy is released — this is the process of nuclear fusion.

questions.q: In the centre of the Sun, what force must protons overcome before the strong nuclear force can fuse them, and at roughly what temperature does fusion become significant?
options: Gravity; about 273 degrees Celsius
The electrostatic repulsive force between positive charges; about 15 million degrees Celsius
Air resistance; about 100 degrees Celsius
The weak nuclear force; about 1 million degrees Celsius
questions.explanation: The strong nuclear force acts over only very short distances within atoms, while the electrostatic repulsive force that exists between all positive charges resists the protons coming together. Protons can fuse only when they have a lot of kinetic energy, which becomes significant at a temperature of about 15 million degrees Celsius in the centre of the Sun.

questions.q: From memory: explain why nuclear fusion requires both extremely high temperature AND extremely high pressure. Address each separately.
keyPoints: Both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel through the long-range Coulomb (electrostatic) force — the Coulomb barrier.
High temperature gives the nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome the Coulomb barrier and approach within ~10⁻¹⁵ m, where the short-range strong nuclear force can take over and bind them.
High pressure and density pack the nuclei close together so that collisions are frequent enough to sustain the reaction.
In a star, gravity supplies the crushing pressure across its enormous mass.
questions.explanation: If you separated the two requirements — temperature for energetic-enough collisions (to beat the Coulomb barrier) and pressure for frequent-enough collisions (to sustain it) — grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Calculate the energy released (in MeV) when deuterium fuses with tritium to form helium-4 plus a neutron, using the light-nuclide atomic masses: deuterium = 2.014102 u, tritium = 3.016049 u, helium-4 = 4.002603 u, neutron = 1.008665 u.
questions.explanation: The mass defect is the total mass of the reactants minus the total mass of the products, taken from the table of atomic masses for light nuclides. Multiplying the mass defect in atomic mass units by 931.5 gives the energy in MeV — about 17.6 MeV per deuterium–tritium event. Do NOT also divide by c²; the 931.5 already carries units of MeV c⁻².

questions.q: The mass defect of a deuterium nucleus is 0.002388 u. Calculate the binding energy of the deuterium nucleus in MeV.
questions.explanation: Using the standard conversion factor where the energy equivalent of a mass of 1 u is 931.5 MeV, the mass defect of the deuterium nucleus, 0.002388 u, gives a binding energy of 0.002388 × 931.5 = 2.224 MeV. This is the energy released if a proton and a neutron combine to form a deuterium nucleus.

questions.q: Whose proposal first identified the fusion of hydrogen to form helium as the energy source of the Sun, and what is the heaviest element stars can build by fusion in their cores?
options: Hans Bethe; uranium
Arthur Eddington; iron
Mark Oliphant; carbon
Cecilia Payne; helium
questions.explanation: Einstein's E = mc² and Cecilia Payne's discovery that the Sun was mostly hydrogen led Arthur Eddington in the 1920s to propose that the fusion of hydrogen to form helium was the missing energy source of the Sun. Mark Oliphant observed fusion in 1932 and Hans Bethe published his calculations in 1939. Elements up to iron can be formed in the cores of stars through fusion, if the star is big enough.

questions.q: From memory: explain the 'iron limit' — why fusion in a star releases energy only up to iron-56.
keyPoints: Iron-56 sits at the very top of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve — it is the most tightly bound, most stable nucleus.
Fusing light nuclei climbs UP the curve toward iron, so the product is more tightly bound, has less mass, and energy is released.
Fusing nuclei PAST iron would give a product lower on the curve (less tightly bound, more mass), so energy must be put in rather than released.
Therefore iron is the heaviest element a star can build by ordinary energy-releasing fusion.
questions.explanation: The same curve that enables fusion on the way up also forbids it past the peak. If you linked iron-56 being the most tightly bound nucleus to fusion past it consuming energy, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: Comparing the energy released per unit mass by fusion, fission and the combustion of fossil fuels, what is the correct order from greatest to least?
options: Fossil-fuel combustion > fission > fusion
Fission > fusion > fossil-fuel combustion
Fusion > fission > fossil-fuel combustion
Fusion = fission, both far less than combustion
questions.explanation: Per unit mass the order is fusion > fission > chemical combustion ('Fusion Feeds the Cosmos'). Although a single fission event (~200 MeV) releases more than a single fusion event (~17.6 MeV), fusion involves only a few nucleons on the steep light end of the binding-energy curve, so per nucleon it releases more. Both nuclear processes dwarf chemical burning, which only rearranges electrons (~a few eV per atom).

questions.q: Explain why nuclear fusion requires extremely high temperatures and pressures. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel each other through the long-range electrostatic, or Coulomb, force — the Coulomb barrier. For fusion to occur, the nuclei must be brought close enough, within about 10⁻¹⁵ m, for the short-range strong nuclear force to overcome that repulsion and bind them together. Overcoming the Coulomb barrier requires the nuclei to collide with very high kinetic energy, and since temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, this demands an extremely high temperature — around 15 million kelvin in the Sun's core. High pressure and density are also required so that collisions occur frequently enough to sustain the reaction.

criteria.descriptor: Names the electrostatic/Coulomb repulsion between the positive nuclei as the barrier.
States the short-range strong nuclear force must take over once nuclei are within ~10⁻¹⁵ m.
Links high temperature to the kinetic energy needed to overcome the Coulomb barrier.
Explains high pressure/density gives frequent enough collisions to sustain the reaction.

questions.explanation: The mark-earning moves are: name the Coulomb barrier, name the short-range strong force, link temperature to kinetic energy, and use pressure for collision frequency. 'Fusion needs heat to make nuclei join' names no force and scores almost nothing.
